issues.description: The entire results section is based on randomized dummy data generated by Qualtrics, not actual participant responses. All statistical findings, effect sizes, p-values, and conclusions are meaningless artifacts of random data. The manuscript presents these results as if they are interpretable findings, including drawing conclusions in the abstract (e.g., 'found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning') and interpreting post-hoc tests. This fundamentally undermines the entire paper as a scientific contribution.
issues.quote: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.subcategory: Abstract reports conclusions from dummy data
issues.description: The abstract presents substantive conclusions drawn from the randomized dummy dataset as if they were real findings. This is misleading to any reader who does not notice the embedded warnings. The abstract states support for hypotheses about perceived impact of donation based on random data.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. To extend the replication, we added the 'perceived impact of donation' as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect. Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The procedures state that participants 'selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions,' which means there is no random assignment. This fundamentally undermines the experimental design, making it impossible to draw causal inferences. The original study used random assignment. Self-selection introduces severe confounds as participants who choose different conditions likely differ systematically.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The authors merged Studies 1 and 3 into a single experiment, changing the design from two separate between-subjects experiments to one combined experiment. This introduces the intervention manipulation to the joint condition (which was not present in the original Study 3), fundamentally altering the comparison structure. The joint condition in the original study had no intervention group, so adding one changes what is being tested and makes direct comparison to the original findings problematic.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect, indicated in the imaginary donation to corresponding victims across conditions. The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.description: The original study gave participants $5 in one-dollar bills and measured actual donation behavior. The replication uses hypothetical/imaginary donation, which is a well-known source of hypothetical bias. This is a significant deviation that could substantially affect results, as hypothetical willingness to donate often differs from actual donation behavior.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Change from lab to online setting
issues.description: The original study was conducted in-person at a university student center where participants physically received money and could donate it. The replication is conducted online via MTurk. This changes the social context, demand characteristics, and ecological validity of the donation decision substantially.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The manuscript describes the design as 'a single within-subject design' but the original studies used between-subjects designs, and the rest of the manuscript (random assignment to conditions, between-subjects ANOVA) implies a between-subjects design. This is a fundamental inconsistency in describing the experimental design.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.description: The dummy data shows a mean age of 67.80 with SD of 30.10 and an age range of 18-120. An age of 120 is biologically implausible, and the mean age of ~68 is unrealistic for an MTurk sample (typical mean age is ~35-40). This highlights that the dummy data is clearly not representative of any real population and should not be interpreted.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males)

issues.description: The results section interprets statistically significant findings from random data as if they are meaningful. For example, the significant effect of identifiability on donation (p=.028) and the interaction effect (p=.015) from random data are discussed substantively. With N=1000 and random data, some spurious significant results are expected by chance alone, yet these are interpreted as supporting hypotheses.
issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.

issues.description: The post-hoc test finds that participants in the statistical victim condition donated MORE than those in the identifiable victim condition, which is the opposite of the identifiable victim effect (Hypothesis 1).
